topics: 🏰 What Counts as a 'House' in a Walled City — presses, bathhouses, towers, and dovecotes, but not fields
🧱 A House Built Into the Wall Itself — Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon, and Rahab's house in Jericho
📜 Which Cities Qualify — walled since Joshua's day, not merely roofs-as-wall, not Tiberias
🤔 The Jerusalem Puzzle — the mishna lists it, but a baraita says its houses are never sold in perpetuity
⏳ Did the Original Conquest's Sanctity Ever Lapse? — Ezra's return, Sukkot, and counting the Jubilee again

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Defining a Walled City
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 32a–32b
overview.hebrewSource: כׇּל שֶׁהוּא לִפְנִים מִן הַחוֹמָה — הֲרֵי הוּא כְּבָתֵּי עָרֵי חוֹמָה, חוּץ מִן הַשָּׂדוֹת
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Having established the one-year redemption rule for a walled-city house, the daf now asks exactly what structures and which cities qualify. A new mishna extends the category to olive presses, bathhouses, towers, dovecotes, and other structures within the wall (but not fields), debates a house built directly into the wall itself, and then lists specific cities recognized as walled since the days of Joshua. A sharp contradiction emerges over whether Jerusalem itself is included, and the daf closes with a sweeping question: did the sanctity Joshua's conquest gave the land ever lapse during the Babylonian exile, requiring Ezra's generation to renew it?

slides.title: 🏰 What Structures Count as a 'House'?
slides.subtitle: New mishna: the category extends well beyond literal houses — almost

boxes.title: Included (All Opinions)
items: Olive presses, bathhouses, towers, dovecotes, pits, ditches, caves
Derived from 'that is in the walled city' — anything located within the city

boxes.title: Disputed
items: Fields inside the wall: R' Yehuda excludes them ('house' implies containing items); R' Meir includes them too
A quarry or sand-bed (cholsit u-metzula): R' Meir treats it like a house; R' Yehuda treats it like a field

slides.title: 🧱 A House Built INTO the Wall
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon read the same biblical verse two ways

lines.speaker: R' Yehuda
lines.text: A house built directly into the city wall is NOT treated as a walled-city house — it isn't really 'in the city.'

lines.speaker: R' Shimon
lines.text: It IS included — the wall's outer face counts as the house's own wall, making it fully part of the city.

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan
lines.text: Both derive their view from the same verse about Rahab in Jericho: 'her house was upon the side of the wall, and she dwelt upon the wall' (Joshua 2:15).

lines.speaker: The split
lines.text: R' Shimon reads it plainly — her house was attached to the wall, inside the city. R' Yehuda reads 'she dwelt upon the wall' as meaning she lived IN the wall itself, not in the city it enclosed.

slides.title: 📜 New Mishna: Which Cities Actually Qualify
slides.subtitle: Walled 'since the days of Joshua, son of Nun' — a demanding historical standard
rows: Not merely a city whose houses' rooftops form a continuous 'roof-wall' (shur igar)
Excludes Tiberias, whose 'wall' on one side was simply the sea
At least three courtyards of two houses each
Walled specifically since Joshua's conquest — not merely walled at some later point
Reading לוֹא (with an alef) as 'does not,' a city that had a wall back then but lacks one now STILL qualifies
Old fortress of Tzippori, Gush Ḥalav, old Yodfat, Gamla, Gedod, Ḥadid, Ono, Jerusalem

slides.title: 🤔 Does Jerusalem Actually Qualify?
slides.subtitle: The mishna lists it — but another baraita seems to say otherwise
slides.label: The contradiction:
slides.text: The mishna names Jerusalem among the cities walled since Joshua's day. But a baraita elsewhere teaches 'ten things were said about Jerusalem,' including that houses there are never sold in perpetuity after a year — directly contradicting the mishna! Two resolutions are offered: Rabbi Yoḥanan says the mishna means a city like Jerusalem (equally walled since Joshua) but not Jerusalem itself, which has its own unique exemption; Rav Ashi suggests instead — as with the two places called Kadesh — that there were simply two different towns named Jerusalem in Judea, and only one carries the special exemption.
slides.hebrewSource: עֲשָׂרָה דְּבָרִים נֶאֶמְרוּ בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם, אֵין הַבַּיִת חָלוּט בָּהּ

slides.title: ⏳ Did the Land's Original Sanctity Lapse?
slides.subtitle: A sweeping dispute traced through Ezra's return from Babylon

steps.content: 1️⃣ One view (R' Yishmael b. R' Yosei): Joshua's conquest sanctified the land only 'for its time' — exile nullified it, so Ezra's generation had to sanctify walled cities anew, which is why the mishna's list is so short
2️⃣ Proof from Nehemiah 8:17: the returnees made sukkot 'as they had not done since the days of Joshua' — implying centuries of lapsed practice, renewed only under Ezra
3️⃣ The opposing view: the original conquest sanctified the land forever — 'since the days of Joshua' in Nehemiah is a comparison of national merit, not a literal gap in sukka-building

4️⃣ Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak's resolution: after the return, they DID count Jubilee cycles — but only to keep the Sabbatical Year's timing accurate, not because the Jubilee's full halakhot were truly in effect (since some tribes remained in exile)

summary.principle: The special one-year redemption rule for a walled-city house extends to many structures within such a city (but not fields), applies only to places genuinely walled since Joshua's conquest, and rests on a deeper unresolved question of whether that conquest-era sanctity of the land was permanent or needed active renewal after the Babylonian exile.

flowSteps.content: 🏰 'House' includes presses, bathhouses, towers, and more — but not fields (disputed)
🧱 A house built into the wall itself: R' Yehuda excludes it, R' Shimon includes it, both from Rahab's house in Jericho

columns.content: 📜 Qualifying cities need a real, full, Joshua-era wall — Tiberias and roof-wall towns don't count
🤔 Jerusalem's own listing conflicts with its special no-forfeiture exemption — resolved two ways

flowSteps.content: ⏳ Whether the land's original sanctity lapsed at exile shapes how these cities were even identified after the return
🎓 Key Principle: a halakhic category as concrete as 'a walled city' still depends on centuries-deep questions of history, geography, and the endurance of sanctity itself

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, which structures inside a walled city are subject to the same redemption rules as houses, and what is universally excluded?
o: Only literal houses qualify; nothing else is included
Olive presses, bathhouses, towers, dovecotes, pits, and caves are included; fields are excluded (though Rabbi Meir disputes this)
Only fields qualify, not any buildings
Everything inside the wall is excluded except houses
quiz.e: The Gemara derives from 'that is in the walled city' that structures like olive presses, bathhouses, towers, and dovecotes are included, while 'house' itself is used to exclude fields — though Rabbi Meir disagrees and includes fields too.

quiz.q: What is the basis of the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon regarding a house built directly into a city's wall?
o: They disagree about the wall's construction materials
Both interpret the same verse about Rahab's house in Jericho differently — Rabbi Shimon reads it as inside the city, Rabbi Yehuda as literally part of the wall and thus not 'in the city'
They disagree only about the house's monetary value
The dispute concerns houses outside city walls entirely
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan explains both opinions derive from Joshua 2:15's description of Rahab's house 'upon the side of the wall' — Rabbi Shimon reads this as being inside the city, while Rabbi Yehuda reads 'she dwelt upon the wall' as living in the wall structure itself, separate from the city.

quiz.q: Why does the mishna exclude Tiberias from the category of cities 'walled since the days of Joshua,' even though it has protective boundaries?
o: Because Tiberias was built after Joshua's era entirely
Because the verse requires the wall to fully surround ('saviv') the city, and Tiberias's sea served as its wall on one side instead of an actual wall
Because Tiberias never had any protective boundary at all
Because Tiberias's population was too small
quiz.e: The Gemara derives from 'saviv' (surrounding) that a city needs to be fully encircled by an actual wall; Tiberias, whose sea substituted for a wall on one side, does not meet this requirement.

quiz.q: What is the contradiction the Gemara raises about Jerusalem's inclusion in the mishna's list of walled cities?
o: The mishna never actually mentions Jerusalem

The mishna lists Jerusalem as qualifying, but another baraita states that among 'ten things said about Jerusalem,' houses there are never sold in perpetuity, seemingly excluding it from this very rule
Jerusalem is said to have no wall at all
The contradiction concerns Jerusalem's Jubilee status, not walled cities
quiz.e: The baraita's list of Jerusalem's ten unique features includes that its houses are never forfeited permanently after a year, directly contradicting the mishna's inclusion of Jerusalem among ordinary walled cities — resolved by positing either a different, comparable city or two distinct towns named Jerusalem.

quiz.q: According to Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak, why did the returnees from Babylonian exile count Jubilee cycles even though the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh remained in exile (which should nullify the Jubilee)?
o: They counted Jubilees to fully reinstate every halakha of the Jubilee Year
They counted Jubilee cycles solely to keep the timing of the Sabbatical Year accurate, not because the full halakhot of the Jubilee Year were actually in effect
They did not count Jubilee cycles at all after the return
They counted Jubilees only for houses in walled cities
quiz.e: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak resolves the difficulty by explaining that counting to the fiftieth year after the return was done purely to keep Sabbatical Year cycles properly timed, even though the Jubilee Year's own halakhot did not actually apply, since not all tribes had returned to the land.
